notable_anecdotes: Joseph Bernstein's handwritten trust declaration dated April 4, 1982 on Manila Peninsula Hotel stationery -- stating he would act as trustee for Marcos and solely per Marcos's instructions for the Crown Building in New York -- discovered among the first post-EDSA documents; without it, the legal link to Marcos's New York real estate would have been impossible to prove.

The multilayer concealment structure: Crown Building in New York titled in a Netherlands Antilles corporation, in turn owned by Panamanian corporations with bearer shares transferable without registration.

Former PCGG Chairman Jovito Salonga revealing the New York real estate concealment scheme in the Lindenmere estate case -- the PCGG chairman as the primary source of the plunder-documentation narrative.

Galman v. Sandiganbayan's finding that the prosecution and the justices who tried the Aquino-Galman case 'acted under the compulsion of some pressure which proved to be beyond their capacity to resist' -- one of the sharpest judicial indictments of a co-equal branch's coercion of the judiciary.

one_paragraph_summary: Responding to reader requests -- especially from history teachers -- for additional SC jurisprudence documenting Marcos's ill-gotten wealth beyond the cases discussed on February 26, Panganiban surveys four categories of decisions. First, the forfeiture cases: Republic v. Sandiganbayan (July 15, 2003) forfeited $658.175 million from Swiss banks; Marcos Jr. v. Republic (April 25, 2012) forfeited $3.37 million. Second, the regime characterizations: Yuchengco v. Sandiganbayan (January 20, 2006), citing PCGG v. Pena (April 12, 1988), described the Marcos rule as 'a well-entrenched plundering regime of twenty years' marked by 'organized pillage'; Licaros v. Sandiganbayan (October 18, 2004) called it 'a dark chapter in our history'; Republic v. Tuvera (February 16, 2007) described it as a regime of 'national trauma.' Third, the concealment technique: former PCGG Chairman Jovito Salonga revealed in the New York real estate case that Marcos owned the Crown Building through a Netherlands Antilles corporation, owned in turn by Panamanian corporations with untraceable bearer shares -- discoverable only because of the Bernstein handwritten trust declaration dated April 4, 1982 on Manila Peninsula Hotel stationery, found among the first post-EDSA documents. Fourth and most damning, Galman v. Sandiganbayan (September 12, 1986) found that Marcos -- code named 'Olympus' -- stage-managed the Aquino-Galman murder trial in a 'scripted and pre-determined manner' that pre-determined the acquittal of the accused, acting through pressure that the prosecution and judges 'proved to be beyond their capacity to resist' -- conduct the Court found had 'no parallel and precedent in our annals and jurisprudence.'
